passage: My cousin Anand used to point and shout "ba-ba-da!" at everything. When I visited this month, he tugged my dupatta toward the fridge and said, "Milk." Later he held up his empty cup: "More milk!" His mother laughed. At bath time he said, "No bath," and ran behind the curtain. I'm Deepika, and I don't know exactly what goes on in his head, but his words got him what he wanted far quicker than pointing ever did.

qa.q: What did Anand say when he held up his empty cup?
qa.a: He said, "More milk!"

qa.q: How did Anand seem to feel about bath time when he said "No bath" and hid?
qa.a: He seemed reluctant and cross about the bath, so he said "No bath" and hid behind the curtain to avoid it.

qa.q: How could Anand's family encourage more words?
qa.a: They can answer his words quickly, repeat them back a little longer, like "More milk, please", and give him time to talk.

qa.q: How does Deepika see the change in Anand?
qa.a: She notices his words work better than pointing did, but admits she can't be sure what he is thinking.

grounding: Shows a toddler moving from babble to single words and short phrases that get his needs met.

passage: First week: Jomon, eighteen months, points at the banana bunch and says, "Ba! Ba!" Tarun, his father, offers a biscuit; Jomon wails and points harder. Tarun asks, "Banana?" and Jomon goes quiet. Two weeks later, Jomon says, "Nana," and Tarun hands one over. A month on, at breakfast, Jomon pushes his plate away. "Nana, Appa. Want nana."

qa.q: What did Tarun first offer instead of a banana?
qa.a: A biscuit.

qa.q: Why did Jomon wail when he got the biscuit?
qa.a: He was frustrated because he wanted the banana and his sound wasn't understood.

qa.q: What helped Jomon move from "Ba" to a real word?
qa.a: Tarun naming the fruit, "Banana?", gave him a clear word to copy.

qa.q: How is breakfast different for Tarun a month later?
qa.a: He no longer has to guess; Jomon tells him in a short sentence what he wants.

grounding: Shows a toddler progressing over weeks from a babbled sound to a word and a short sentence to ask for food.

passage: At the crowded vegetable market in Chennai, Shankar, two, rides on his mother Chandrika's hip. He spots a man selling balloons. "Ball-oon! Amma, ball-oon!" She keeps walking. He pats her cheek. "Amma. Red one. Please." Chandrika stops, surprised; he has never said please before. She buys one red balloon and holds the string for him. "Mine," he says, reaching up high.

qa.q: What colour of balloon did Shankar ask for?
qa.a: A red one.

qa.q: Why was Chandrika surprised?
qa.a: Shankar had never said please before, so the new word caught her off guard.

qa.q: What could Chandrika do to keep Shankar using new words?
qa.a: She can reply when he talks in short phrases and name things around them in the market.

qa.q: What would change if Shankar could only point and cry?
qa.a: Chandrika might not know what he wanted in the busy market, and both could end up frustrated.

grounding: Shows a toddler using a short sentence to ask for what he wants in a busy city market.

passage:
"Siddharth, what do you want?"
"Mmm-ba!"
Pankaj, the boy's father, points. "Ball?"
"Ba!"
"Say ball."
"Bah!" Siddharth, eighteen months, stretches his arms toward the shelf.
Pankaj brings it down. "Here's the ball."
Siddharth hugs it. "More ba!" he says, pointing at a second ball.
"More ball? You said more!"
Siddharth grins and bounces.

qa.q: What did Siddharth point at when he said "More ba"?
qa.a: He pointed at a second ball.

qa.q: What does Siddharth's bouncing and grinning suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he is happy and proud that his father understood him.

qa.q: How does Pankaj help Siddharth's speech?
qa.a: He repeats the correct word, 'ball', and praises Siddharth when he joins words.

qa.q: What would change if Pankaj ignored Siddharth's early sounds?
qa.a: Siddharth might feel less encouraged to keep trying to use words to ask for things.

grounding: Shows a toddler moving from babbling toward functional words and a two-word phrase to ask for things.

passage:
Daycare note, Sumit (teacher), Friday.

Amandeep, two, used a short sentence today: "Me want water." Until last month she mostly pointed and said "uh-uh." This week she's also said "Mama gone" and "No sleep." When I didn't understand "ba-na," she pulled me to the fruit basket. I repeated "banana" and she said "nana!" I'll keep narrating our routines and give her time to answer. 👍

qa.q: What short sentence did Amandeep use today?
qa.a: She said, "Me want water."

qa.q: Why did Amandeep pull Sumit to the fruit basket?
qa.a: She wanted Sumit to understand her and was determined to get the banana.

qa.q: How is Sumit supporting Amandeep's speech?
qa.a: By repeating words clearly, narrating routines and giving her time to answer.

qa.q: How might Amandeep's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They'd likely be pleased to hear her moving from pointing to short sentences.

grounding: Shows a teacher noting a toddler moving from pointing and babbling to short sentences about her needs.
